extracted.intended_audience: IP practitioners, in-house counsel, rights holders and applicants dealing with intellectual property in the Philippines
extracted.subtask_description: A country-specific Q&A overview of Philippine intellectual property laws, registration procedures, enforcement remedies, timelines, fees, and practice points relevant to patents, utility models, trademarks, designs, copyrights, plant varieties and related IP rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Section 21 of the Intellectual Property Code a patentable invention is any technical solution of a problem in any field of human activity which is new, involves an inventive step, and has industrial applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May relate to a product or process as well as improvements made thereon. Observations in writing on patentability may be presented within six months from publication; substantive examination occurs after request or when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Any technical solution of a problem in any field of human activity which is new and has industrial applicability; it does not need to involve any inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility models may relate to product or process and improvements. Term is seven (7) years from filing and is not extendible. Utility models do not undergo substantive examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade secret recognition and protection
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no specific statutory definition of 'trade secrets' but the IP Code recognizes protection of undisclosed information as an IP right; courts have used Black's Law Dictionary definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of secrets with abuse of office is penalized under Articles 291–292 RPC. Practical protection relies on contracts, confidentiality measures and criminal/penal provisions for wrongful disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark registrability and definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A mark is 'any visible sign capable of distinguishing the goods (trademark) or services (service mark) of an enterprise' (Section 121.1 IP Code).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes stamped/marked containers. Sound and scent marks are not yet registrable in the Philippines. Examiner may require sworn statements or affidavit of good faith when veracity is doubted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of unfair competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 168.2 IP Code provides a cause of action for unfair competition when a person employs deception or other means contrary to good faith in passing off goods or services; Article 28 New Civil Code gives broader relief against unjust or oppressive methods causing unfair competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of fraud is essential under Article 168.2; unfair competition claims may be broader under civil code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical indications and collective marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical indications are protected under the IP Code and may be registered as a collective mark, though not separately defined in the IP Code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use collective mark registration mechanisms to protect geographic indications in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright subsistence and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protects original literary, artistic, scholarly and scientific works from the moment of creation; database rights are protected as 'compilations' original by selection/arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copyright registration is unnecessary for protection but works may be deposited with the IPOPHL online for evidentiary advantages; ECRD issued on payment and confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial design registrability and term
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial design: any composition of lines or colours or three-dimensional form giving special appearance to a product (Section 112 IP Code). Term: 5 years from filing, renewable twice for a total maximum of 15 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renewal requires fees (can be paid 12 months prior); six-month grace period to pay with surcharge. Industrial design registration may be cancelled if subject matter not registrable, not new, or extends beyond original content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layout-design (topography) protection and term
rubrics_metrics.description: Layout-design of integrated circuits is the three-dimensional disposition of elements and interconnections (Section 112); protection term is 10 years from commencement of protection, with specific rules on start date (first commercial exploitation or filing date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If commercially exploited, application must be filed within two years of first exploitation to preserve earlier start date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant variety eligibility and terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Plant under Plant Variety Protection Act includes terrestrial and aquatic flora; a 'variety' is a plant grouping definable by genotype characteristics. Term: 25 years for trees/vines and 20 years for other plants from grant of certificate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must submit propagating material samples; substantive examination applies. Oppositions may be filed within 60 days from publication in Plant Variety Gazette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term
rubrics_metrics.description: A regular patent term is twenty (20) years from the filing date (PCT patents counted from international filing date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annual fees (annuities) must be paid within periods required by the IP Code to maintain term; failure to pay leads to withdrawal/ lapse with limited remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark registration term and use declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark registration is valid for 10 years, subject to required declarations of actual use and evidence as prescribed by the IP Code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opposition period after publication is 30 days (extendible). Renewal fees and use declarations must be monitored to avoid vulnerability to cancellation (non-use for three uninterrupted years grounds for cancellation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright term duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protection generally lasts for the lifetime of the author plus fifty (50) years after the author's death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivative works and compilations have protection scope per selection/arrangement originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership rules for IP created in employment or commission
rubrics_metrics.description: The first owner is the registrant, author, inventor, designer or breeder. If created in course of employment, the IP belongs to the employee if the work is not part of duties; otherwise owner is employer unless contrary agreement. Commissioned works belong to commissioning party unless agreement states otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should record ownership and have written agreements to avoid disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may apply and formal filing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals and juridical entities may apply for patents, utility models, industrial designs; foreigners/non-residents must appoint a local agent. Applications are submitted via IPOPHL e-Services portal with required documents and fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications undergo formality examination after filing. For large file sizes (>10MB) or exceptional circumstances, alternate filing methods (mail, courier, other electronic means) are permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent publication, third-party observations and substantive examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular patents are published in the IPO E-Gazette after 18 months from filing. Any person may present observations in writing concerning patentability within six (6) months from publication of the application; substantive examination proceeds thereafter (or when requested).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations are communicated to applicant who may comment within 30 days. Requests for conferences by interested parties are permitted subject to fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive examination exemptions for utility models and industrial designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility models and industrial designs do not undergo substantive examination (only formality examination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their term timelines are faster (typical 6–12 months) but lack of substantive examination affects post-grant challenge procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark examination, publication and opposition procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark examiner reviews filing for filing and registrability requirements; if registrable, notice of allowance issued and upon fee payment the mark is published for opposition. Opposer has 30 days post-publication to oppose (extendible by 45 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no opposition or extension filed, mark is deemed registered the day after the opposition period expires. Examiner may request sworn statements if factual veracity is in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timelines for typical registration procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: If no opposition: trademark registration usually concluded within 8–12 months. Patents: typically 2–5 years from filing (complexity dependent). Utility models and industrial designs: typically 6–12 months provided formality compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timelines are subject to procedural events (opposition, substantive examination requests, complexity) and system availability (e-filing downtime exceptions exist).

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party participation rights during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Third parties can oppose trademarks within the prescribed opposition period; for patents, third parties may submit observations in writing within six months from publication and may request conferences at IPOPHL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All observations are acknowledged and communicated to applicant; applicant has opportunity to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal routes for refusals
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark refusals: appeal to Director of Bureau of Trademarks within two months; adverse Director decisions may be appealed to Director General or motion for reconsideration filed within 30 days. Patent refusals: appealable to Director of Bureau of Patents within two months (non-extendible); further appeal to Director General within one month of Director decision; then Court of Appeals and Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motions for reconsideration are not allowed for patent Director decisions; procedural time limits are strict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee structures and payment requirements (patents, utility models, industrial designs, trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed official fees apply for filings and annuities: examples include patent filing fees (small entity ₱2,020.00 for up to 5 claims inclusive of 1% legal research fee), additional claim fees, priority claim fees; annuity ranges (small entity ₱1,565.50 to ₱31,534.22 for 5th to 20th year). Utility model and industrial design application and renewal fees specified; trademark basic fees per class and publication fees differ for big/small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application is subject to full payment of filing fee and first publication fee upon filing (Memorandum Circular No. 2022-016). Late renewals typically incur a surcharge (e.g., 50% for industrial designs). Monitor fee schedules closely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and remedies for failure to pay renewal/annuity fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to pay annual or renewal fees on due dates results in withdrawal of the patent application/registration and industrial design registrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedy: pay within grace period plus surcharge — patents: six months from publication of non-payment in IPO E-Gazette; industrial designs: six months from expiration of term. Late payments involve surcharge/penalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment and transfer formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Recordal of assignments required: deed of assignment must be duly notarized and apostilled/authenticated; power of attorney for local agent; optional IPO deed of assignment form available. For plant varieties, original/certified and duplicate copies of deed required for recording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments not recorded with IPO are void against third parties. Transfers by merger require documents evidencing transfer (e.g., extract of commercial register) with English translation if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to record assignments/ consequences of non-recordal
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106 (patents/utility models/industrial design) and Section 149.4 (trademarks) require recordal of assignments and transfers with the IPO; assignments not recorded shall be void against third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record agreements promptly to protect rights versus third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing formalities and mandatory/prohibited clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: To license an IP right, parties must submit a request letter, licensing agreement and notarized application form. Trademark or patent license agreements need not be recorded if they conform with mandatory clauses (Section 88) and do not include prohibited clauses (Section 87).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandatory clauses include arbitration clause, applicability of Philippine law, venue for litigation, and licensor bearing Philippine taxes related to technology transfer. License lacking mandatory clauses or containing prohibited clauses is unenforceable against third parties and must be approved/registered with DITTB as an exempt agreement where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark license quality control requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing rules require trademark license agreements to provide effective control by the licensor of the quality of the licensee's goods or services; absent quality control or its effective exercise, the license is not valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may request preliminary DITTB review and obtain a certificate of clearance prior to recordal; clearance is required prior to recordal of trademark or patent license agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive vs non-exclusive licensee enforcement rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Rights between licensor and licensee are contractually determined; absent contrary provision, the licensor may grant further licenses to third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft license clauses carefully to allocate enforcement rights and remedies between parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal sanctions for IP infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent: first offense not punishable by imprisonment; repeat offense imprisonment 6 months–3 years and fine ₱100,000–₱300,000. Trademark: imprisonment 2–5 years and fine ₱50,000–₱200,000 (Section 170). Copyright: escalating penalties—first offense imprisonment 1–3 years + fine ₱50,000–₱150,000, second offense 3+ years + higher fines, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal cases are commenced by information filed by the Prosecutor after a verified complaint and preliminary investigation; penalties increase for repeat offenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil, administrative and alternative enforcement options
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil actions (regional trial courts designated as special commercial courts), administrative proceedings (IPOPHL Bureau of Legal Affairs), criminal prosecutions, IPOPHL arbitration under Office Order No. 61, and IPR Enforcement Office orders are available remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative infringement actions require damages claimed of at least ₱200,000 to be filed with IPO-BLA. Parties may opt for arbitration per IPOPHL rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical duration and estimated costs of enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Bureau of Legal Affairs cases: typically 8 months to 2 years, legal fees approx. US$5,000–US$10,000. Local courts (civil/criminal): 2–3 years, legal fees approx. US$5,000–US$20,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs and timelines vary with complexity, relief sought, and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction, procedure and timing in court proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Special commercial courts of the Regional Trial Courts have jurisdiction over infringement cases where elements of infringement occurred. Criminal prosecutions require preliminary investigation and information filing; civil complaints must include supporting evidence and judicial affidavits under 2020 IPR Rules. Timelines provided for arraignment, pre-trial, mediation, evidence presentation (each party 30 days), memoranda (30 days), and decision promulgation (60 days after submission). Appeals to Court of Appeals available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules allow submission on position papers; extraterritorial service of summons permitted as provided by treaty; injunctive relief may be executory pending appeal unless otherwise ordered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs recording and border measures
rubrics_metrics.description: IP rights may be recorded with Bureau of Customs for a two-year period. BOC may issue alert or hold orders and conduct inspections of shipments suspected of containing infringing goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recording with BOC facilitates border enforcement; renew recording as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory mediation and non-court dispute mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative complaints and IPO-BLA appellate proceedings require mandatory mediation per IPOPHL Rules. Civil and criminal actions require court-annexed mediation with Judicial Dispute Resolution (JDR) available if mediation fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should expect and prepare for mediation/JDR as part of the process; these steps are mandatory in many forums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing trademark infringement: confusing similarity (dominancy test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark infringement requires establishment of confusing similarity. The court applies the dominancy test (adopted in Kolin Electronics Co. Inc v. Kolin Philippines International, Inc) focusing on dominant features, visual/aural/connotative comparisons and overall impression; likelihood of confusion is presumed for identical marks on identical goods/services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual confusion need not be shown. Use market surveys, evidence of distinctiveness and primary significance to relevant public to prove or rebut likelihood of confusion; the holistic test has been abandoned in favor of dominancy test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for proving copyright infringement and ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright is presumed to subsist in the work and that copyright belongs to complainant who claims ownership through affidavit evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depositing works and maintaining records assists evidentiary burden; affidavit ownership and registration/deposit (ECRD) strengthen claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for proving patent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent infringement requires proof that essential or substantial features of the patented invention are appropriated or that the accused device performs same function/achieves same result by identical or substantially identical means; principle/mode of operation must be substantially the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants may counter with invalidity arguments or show lack of equivalence (function-means-result). Courts may appoint technical experts or committee of experts to advise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence quantum across forums
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil actions require preponderance of evidence; administrative actions require substantial evidence (relevant evidence a reasonable mind might accept); criminal actions require proof beyond reasonable doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust evidence strategy accordingly; administrative complaints have lower evidentiary threshold but are subject to mandatory mediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-appointed and party experts; technical fact-finding
rubrics_metrics.description: Court may appoint an expert or order a committee of three experts in patent cases (motu proprio or upon motion). Parties may present their own expert witnesses subject to cross-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties can move for appointment or present competing experts; technical committees provide specialized advice on complex inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery, disclosure and evidence-obtaining mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Modes of discovery under the Rules of Court (depositions, interrogatories, production/inspection, requests for admission) are available; compliance generally required within 10 calendar days of receipt unless objections filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions for non-compliance exist. Ex parte writs of search and seizure are available; courts can order preservation, inspection, copying and seizure of documents and articles in IP actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and scrutiny of evidence under 2020 IPR Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: 2020 IPR Rules provide evidentiary guidelines: fraudulent intent need not be established in infringement (good faith not a defense unless claiming prior user), foreign official documents per treaty admissible, electronic documents admissible if compliant with Rules on Electronic Evidence; market surveys admissible to prove distinctiveness or likelihood of confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare electronic evidence to be compliant with electronic evidence rules; submit market surveys and other consumer perception evidence when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available defenses to infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Defenses include proof confusion is unlikely (trademark), prior use in good faith, innocent infringer (printing businesses), publisher/distributor protections, laches/acquiescence, fair use (copyright), patent invalidity, failure of doctrine of equivalents (function-means-result), surrender/lapse/expiration of patent, and plant variety specific defenses (non-infringement, not distinct/novel, prior adverse right).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good faith alone is not a defense in many infringement actions; defendants often raise invalidity to counter patent/utility model claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may challenge rights and when
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents: any person may present observations within six months from publication. Trademarks: any person who would be damaged may file opposition within 30 days of publication or petition for cancellation during subsistence (certain grounds limited to 5 years for confusing similarity). Plant varieties: opposition within 60 days of publication. Utility models and industrial designs cannot be challenged by third party pre-grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different IP rights have different challenge windows and forums (IPOPHL BLA for cancellations/oppositions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds and forum for cancellation/invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Forum: IPO Bureau of Legal Affairs for petitions to cancel patents/trademarks; courts for certain ownership disputes. Grounds for patent cancellation: lack of novelty/patentability, insufficient disclosure, contrary to public order/morality. Utility model grounds: not registrable or description/claims/ drawings insufficient, owner not maker/successor. Industrial design grounds: not registrable, not new, or extends beyond original application. Trademark cancellation grounds: genericness, abandonment, registration obtained fraudulently, misrepresentation of source, non-use for 3+ years, confusing similarity to earlier mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some grounds may require court forum (e.g., entitlement/true inventor) and certain combined grounds may preclude separate court filing if raised administratively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other mechanisms to limit or remove IP effects (licences, declaratory relief)
rubrics_metrics.description: IP rights may be exploited or limited via license agreements; declaratory relief and cancellation proceedings are available to remove or limit IP rights under prescribed grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensing remains a practical method to resolve disputes and avoid costly litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies (interim and final) in infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Available remedies include preliminary and final injunctions, damages (including reasonable profits), destruction of infringing goods/materials, fines, impounding of sales invoices and documents, and ex parte writs of search and seizure for inspection and seizure of specified documents/articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may require bond conditioned to pay costs/damages arising from issuance of writ; seek urgent ex parte relief where imminent harm exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs, security for costs and recovery of attorney's fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing/investigation/storage/attorney fees range approx. US$5,000–US$20,000 depending on forum; attorney's fees and costs may be awarded per Article 2208 New Civil Code. A bond may be required for writs of search and seizure to cover defendant's damages from wrongful issuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider likely cost exposure and possibility of cost recovery when deciding forum and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: COVID-19 related procedural and filing changes
rubrics_metrics.description: IPOPHL shifted to mandatory electronic filing and payment for many services (eTMfile, eInventionFile, eUMfFile, eIDFile) and mandatory e-filing of pleadings/motions/appeals in inter partes and IP rights violation cases. Requirement to submit a flash drive/USB in IPCs was suspended; hard copies still required 10 days prior to preliminary conference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memorandum Circulars implemented e-filing and amended rules (e.g., allowing single pleading for oppositions/petitions involving more than one application with same parties). Statutory deadlines largely unchanged but filing modes updated — plan for electronic submission and larger file handling where needed.
